comparisons.title: Billing me softly: How to design targeted energy discounts
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = cost to the Exchequer (printed as costs transferred 'from billpayers to taxpayers')
comparisons.cause: These producers price a wider change than the option, which moves only the remaining 25% of the Renewables Obligation and the Feed-in Tariffs off household electricity bills. The MCS Foundation removes all remaining social and environmental levies and the REA all remaining levies on household electricity bills; Octopus lists the Warm Home Discount, RO, Sizewell C, Network Charging Compensation, AAHEDC and FiT; JRF adds the Warm Home Discount; the Electricity Bills Taskforce adds the Warm Home Discount and the nuclear levy; RF's Power struggle moves the rest of the RO, the FiT, the Warm Home Discount, the nuclear RAB, Network Charging Compensation, the Green Gas Levy and AAHEDC and removes the Carbon Price Support, and its August 'remaining levies' are not listed. They are shown beside the option because its £120 assumption is the size of this wider change (annotation levy-scope-120-assumption).
comparisons.pe_missing: RF does not list its 'remaining levies' here; its Power struggle (March 2026) counts the remaining policy costs as the rest of the RO, the FiT, the Warm Home Discount, the nuclear RAB, Network Charging Compensation, the Green Gas Levy and AAHEDC, more than the option's remaining 25% of the RO and the FiT.

comparisons.locator: paragraph on how the cut is funded

comparisons.title: Trimming the VAT
comparisons.locator: paragraph comparing the VAT cut with levies
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = gain to households (printed as a bill saving)
comparisons.estimate_label: Average gain per household (all households) from the remaining 25% of the RO and the FiT moved to taxation, 2027-28
comparisons.cause: The dashboard does not price the two levies. It sets the cut so that it takes £120 off a typical 2027-28 electricity bill of 2,500 kWh, a figure it takes from press reports with a £3.2bn price tag (LEVY_SAVING_TYPICAL in budget_options.py, citing the Guardian of 6 October and the FT of 11 October 2026), and applies that share, 12.6%, to every GB household's electricity bill. The remaining 25% of the Renewables Obligation and the Feed-in Tariffs are worth far less: CBP prices them together at c. £1.5bn and £53 a household (£780m and £730m), RF at £42 a year and, as mean averages, £26 and £24 a year, Good Energy at £0.61bn and £0.57bn (£20.45 and £19.25 on a typical bill), and HM Treasury's costing of the 75% of the domestic RO already funded (-£2,100m in 2027-28) puts the remaining quarter near £0.7bn. £120 is the size producers give for removing every remaining policy cost: RF's mean of £128 for all of them (Power struggle), the MCS Foundation's average of around £120 (at its archetypes' 3,955 kWh), the REA's £112 for a typical bill. So the option prices that wider change under the narrower label (annotation wider-levy-scope): its £3.83bn is close to RF's £3.75bn for every remaining policy cost plus the Carbon Price Support, and 20-28% above the REA's £3.2bn and the MCS Foundation's just over £3bn. The year does not close the gap: the producers' figures are at 2026 levy rates, the RO part falls in 2027-28 (the Treasury's 75% costing goes from £2,580m in 2026-27 to £2,100m), and the FiT part (£0.57bn in Good Energy's table to c. £0.73bn in CBP's) is too small to make up a difference of about £2.3bn whatever its indexation. RF's £42 is per household and the dashboard's £130 is the mean over all households; the dashboard's own typical-household saving is £120, so the statistic accounts for little of the gap.

comparisons.cause: The dashboard does not price the two levies. It sets the cut so that it takes £120 off a typical 2027-28 electricity bill of 2,500 kWh, a figure it takes from press reports with a £3.2bn price tag (LEVY_SAVING_TYPICAL in budget_options.py, citing the Guardian of 6 October and the FT of 11 October 2026), and applies that share, 12.6%, to every GB household's electricity bill. The remaining 25% of the Renewables Obligation and the Feed-in Tariffs are worth far less: CBP prices them together at c. £1.5bn and £53 a household (£780m and £730m), RF at £42 a year and, as mean averages, £26 and £24 a year, Good Energy at £0.61bn and £0.57bn (£20.45 and £19.25 on a typical bill), and HM Treasury's costing of the 75% of the domestic RO already funded (-£2,100m in 2027-28) puts the remaining quarter near £0.7bn. £120 is the size producers give for removing every remaining policy cost: RF's mean of £128 for all of them (Power struggle), the MCS Foundation's average of around £120 (at its archetypes' 3,955 kWh), the REA's £112 for a typical bill. So the option prices that wider change under the narrower label (annotation wider-levy-scope): its £3.83bn is close to RF's £3.75bn for every remaining policy cost plus the Carbon Price Support, and 20-28% above the REA's £3.2bn and the MCS Foundation's just over £3bn. The year does not close the gap: the producers' figures are at 2026 levy rates, the RO part falls in 2027-28 (the Treasury's 75% costing goes from £2,580m in 2026-27 to £2,100m), and the FiT part (£0.57bn in Good Energy's table to c. £0.73bn in CBP's) is too small to make up a difference of about £2.3bn whatever its indexation. RF's £42 is per household and the dashboard's £130 is the mean over all households; the dashboard's own typical-household saving is £120, so the statistic accounts for little of the gap.

analysis-uk-triple-lock.title: The Burnham plan vs the triple lock

comparisons.title: State Pension uprating (State Pension uprating analysis 2026)
comparisons.locator: Impacts, Table 1: Estimated AME savings of adjusted Triple Lock policy relative to Triple Lock (nominal)
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = increase in AME spending (Table 1: 'negative values denote savings')
comparisons.estimate_label: Expected gross saving, Burnham plan vs triple lock, 2039-40
comparisons.cause: Unexplained; tracked in PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock#13, which says the cause of this gap is not established. A partial account, from measured bills and one paired run rather than matched model runs: DWP's £15bn is for Great Britain. The dashboard sets it beside its UK figure, £11.14bn (26% below), and the results file's Great Britain figure is £10.83bn (28% below). Much of the gap is the size of the pension bill. On any one path the gross saving is a fixed share of the basic and new State Pension bill: the engine fails a run unless every such pension scales by the ratio of the two rules' amounts (engine.py), and the results file's paired run on Microcosm, whose 2026-27 basic and new bill is 10.1% larger, raises the 2039-40 saving by £1.12bn with the share unchanged (expected_value.paired_difference.gross_share_flat_rate_spending_pct: 0.0000001 points). The dashboard's basic and new State Pension spending in Great Britain is 84 to 86% of DWP's figure, which includes payments abroad (flat_rate_bn: 0.856 in 2026-27, 0.837 in 2030-31; coverage.by_year). DWP separates payments abroad (£5.9bn in 2026-27, £6.6bn in 2030-31) only for all State Pension types together, so the like-for-like shortfall is about 10 to 16%. The Enhanced FRS has 11.16m recipients in Great Britain against DWP's 12.15m in 2026-27, and the method grows the survey's own counts by ONS growth rather than matching ONS levels (METHOD.md), so the shortfall carries forward. On the OBR-wedge path the dashboard's 2039-40 State Pension bill under the triple lock is £243.2bn for the UK, 85% of the £286bn the Resolution Foundation cites for that year; RF does not say whether that includes payments abroad, which the survey omits. Taking the bill shortfall out leaves the Great Britain figure about 14 to 19% below DWP's, and the paired Microcosm run, whose basic and new bill is 0.94 of DWP's figure including payments abroad, gives £11.94bn for Great Britain, 20% below: inside the threshold either way. The remainder is consistent with a different uprating path, with Pensim3's projection of the population and pension types after 2030-31, or with DWP's rounding to £1bn, and none of these can be checked. DWP's page says the analysis 'applies a path for uprating' but does not publish it. Asked for its yearly earnings and CPI assumptions, DWP answered that the analysis 'did not use single year assumptions for earnings or prices growth' (HL3774). This is an accounting decomposition from measured bills and one paired run, not the matched full-run counterfactual the analysis's issue #13 asks for.

comparisons.sign_convention: positive = saving
comparisons.cause: RF's 'around £15 billion' reproduces the government's figure. comparisons.title: Triple lock calculator data (the Prime Minister's plan, reform from April 2030)
comparisons.sign_convention: positive = saving (the calculator: 'Positive = cheaper than the Triple Lock')
comparisons.estimate_label: Expected gross saving, Burnham plan vs triple lock, 2031-32
comparisons.cause: Two differences documented in CBP's methodology put its savings above the dashboard's. First, the spending base, which 'the savings scale with'. CBP counts 13.39 million pensioners in 2026 (tool_data.json population: 5.89m new, 7.51m basic), from DWP's caseload, which includes pensioners abroad (CBP leaves only their share out of its tax calculation), against the survey's 11.46m UK recipients (results.json coverage). It prices each at the full weekly rate (£241.30 new, £184.90 basic), which 'ignores partial entitlements'. That makes CBP's base about £146bn in 2026-27 against the dashboard's £115.2bn UK bill, 27% larger: a count 17% higher, and full rates 8 to 9% above survey amounts. By 2039-40 the gap narrows to about 23% at 2026 rates (CBP's 15.05m pensioners against the dashboard's central-path bill deflated by its own triple-lock index). The dashboard's saving is a fixed share of its bill on each path (engine.py), so the base accounts for about 70% of the 2039-40 gap, where CBP's £14.90bn is 34% above the dashboard's £11.14bn. Second, the paths. CBP's baseline is 'the model's own projection of the Triple Lock, not the OBR's forecast, so savings will not match a costing scored against the OBR's Economic and Fiscal Outlook'. CBP says its inflation 'settles too high' (2.9% a year over 2032-49) and its earnings growth is 'too volatile', both raising the savings, while normal shocks understate large inflation surprises, which works the other way ('the net effect is unclear'). The dashboard's paths are shifted so their means match the OBR's March 2026 central path, on which CPI is 2.0% and the earnings input stays below 2.5% for the April 2028 to 2031 rises. On that path the 2.5% floor sets both rules' rise and the plan saves nothing until 2032-33 (central.run.rate_sources, central.run.saving_bn). That is where the early years part most: the dashboard is 59% below CBP in 2031-32 (£0.22bn against £0.53bn) and 37% below in 2032-33.

The report's tax expenditure is New York State personal income tax liability alone, from a study file of full-year resident, part-year resident and nonresident returns. The dashboard's figure is the net budget effect for New York resident households: the change in federal income tax plus state income tax minus household benefits (total_budgetary_impact in scripts/modal_cpid_endpoint.py at 0525a73). Its state income tax includes New York City income tax (state_income_tax_before_refundable_credits lists nyc_income_tax_before_refundable_credits; nyc_taxable_income adds ny_taxable_income), which applies to households the dataset places in the five NYC counties (in_nyc reads county_str); whether the June state file placed households in those counties is not recorded. The run did not save the state-only change (state_tax_change), so the components cannot be separated from results.json.
comparisons.pe_missing: Same reform, year and time basis as ny_dependent_exemption_cost_2026, but not the same quantity: the report's figure is New York State tax on resident and nonresident returns, and the dashboard's is the net change in federal, state and New York City income tax less benefits for resident households (annotation ny-dependent-exemption-scope). The two are 0.7% apart.
